brief.t: Started in 1991 (as Maxi Motors Financial Services) to give loans for Mahindra vehicles to rural buyers; it is part of the Mahindra group and listed in 2006.
Mainly a vehicle lender: about 80% of loans are 'wheels' (cars and utility vehicles, tractors, trucks, used vehicles); the rest is SME loans, personal loans, leasing and home loans.
Raul Rebello, an ex-Axis Bank rural banker, has been MD & CEO since Ramesh Iyer retired in April 2024; Dr Anish Shah (Group CEO of M&M) is Chairman.
Profit is climbing: FY 2025-26 standalone profit was ₹2,782 crore (+19%), and Q2 FY27 (Jul–Sep 2026) profit was ₹882 crore (+55%).
In Aug 2026 the board approved merging its home-loan subsidiary, Mahindra Rural Housing Finance, into the company (proposed from 1 April 2027, approvals pending).

timeline.t: Incorporated as Maxi Motors Financial Services; renamed Mahindra & Mahindra Financial Services in 1992.
Began financing Mahindra utility vehicles, its first loans.
IPO: shares listed on the stock exchanges.

Board approved merging Mahindra Rural Housing Finance into the company.

model.how: Mahindra Finance borrows money from banks and bond investors and lends it, mostly to buy vehicles and tractors, to customers in villages and small towns, many of whom have little credit history. It earns the gap between its loan rates and its borrowing cost, plus fees such as insurance commissions.
flow: Borrows from banks, bonds (NCDs) and deposits
Lends for cars, tractors, trucks, used vehicles and SMEs
Field staff collect repayments, often in villages
Earns interest gap + fees, minus costs and bad loans

points: Vehicle and tractor loans depend on rural incomes, harvests and vehicle sales, so collections can swing with the season.
NBFCs borrow from banks and bond markets, so their cost of funds rises when interest rates go up.
Big theme for interviews: how a vehicle lender grows 'non-wheel' loans such as SME, personal and home loans.

glossary.NBFC: Non-Banking Financial Company: a lender regulated by the RBI that gives loans but cannot take savings or current account deposits like a bank.
glossary.AUM: Assets Under Management: the total loans an NBFC has given out and not yet been repaid. The main size measure for a lender.
glossary.Disbursements: New loans paid out to customers in a period.
glossary.Net profit: What is left after all costs, provisions and taxes. The company's final earnings.
glossary.Net Interest Income: Interest earned on loans minus interest paid on borrowings. A lender's main earning.
glossary.Net interest margin: Net Interest Income as a % of loans or interest-earning assets. Shows how profitable lending is.
glossary.Gross NPA: Loans not repaid for 90+ days (called 'Stage 3' loans by NBFCs), as a % of all loans.
glossary.Net NPA: Bad loans after subtracting the money already set aside (provisions) for them. Lower is better.
glossary.Stage 3 assets: Loans that have stopped paying for 90+ days. NBFCs report Gross and Net Stage 3, similar to banks' NPA.
glossary.Credit cost: Money set aside for bad loans, as a % of average loans. Lower means fewer losses.
glossary.Capital adequacy ratio: The lender's own capital compared with the risk in its loans. RBI requires NBFCs to keep at least 15%.
glossary.Provisions: Money set aside from profit to cover loans that may not be repaid.
glossary.Borrowings: Money an NBFC raises from banks, bonds (NCDs), commercial paper and, for some, public deposits, to lend onward.
glossary.Cost of funds: The average interest an NBFC pays on its borrowings. NBFCs usually pay more than banks, so a strong credit rating matters.
glossary.Credit rating: An agency's grade (e.g. AAA) of how safely a company can repay debt. Higher ratings mean cheaper borrowing.
glossary.Upper Layer NBFC: The largest and most important NBFCs, named by the RBI under its scale-based rules. They face bank-like rules and must list on the stock market within 3 years.
glossary.Return on assets: Net profit as a % of average total assets. Shows how well a lender earns on what it owns.
glossary.Dividend: Part of the profit paid to shareholders, per share.
glossary.Attrition: The % of employees who leave in a year. Also called employee turnover.
glossary.RBI: Reserve Bank of India, which regulates banks and NBFCs in India.
glossary.KYC: Know Your Customer: checking a customer's identity before giving a loan.
glossary.MSME: Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises: small businesses that lenders serve.
glossary.Cross-sell: Selling an extra product (like insurance or a second loan) to an existing customer.
glossary.Co-lending: A bank and an NBFC lending together: the NBFC finds and services the borrower, the bank funds most of the loan.
glossary.IPO: Initial Public Offering: when a company first sells its shares to the public.
glossary.BRSR: Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report: an official yearly report on people, environment and governance that big listed companies must publish.
glossary.Business assets: Mahindra Finance's name for its total loan book (AUM), including leasing.
glossary.Collection efficiency: The share of the money due from borrowers in a period that was actually collected. Close to 100% is good.
glossary.Stage 2 assets: Loans 30 to 90 days late: not yet bad, but a warning sign.
glossary.Merger: Two companies joining into one; here a subsidiary is being folded into its parent.
glossary.Swap ratio: How many shares of the merged company a shareholder of the merging company gets, e.g. 1.8 for every 10.

Marketing.tip: Think about reaching first-time and small-town borrowers through dealers, branches and mobile.

Finance.q: What drove Mahindra Finance's profit growth in Q2 FY27?
Finance.a: Loans grew 15%, the margin held at about 7%, and credit cost was 1.6%, within its 1.3–1.7% target, so profit rose 55% to ₹882 crore (standalone).

Finance.q: What is the difference between Stage 2 and Stage 3 assets?
Finance.a: Stage 2 loans are 30–90 days late (early stress); Stage 3 are over 90 days late (bad loans). Mahindra Finance's Gross Stage 3 was 3.4% in Sep 2026.

Finance.q: Why does a rise in interest rates hurt an NBFC?
Finance.a: NBFCs borrow from banks and bond markets; when rates rise their cost of funds goes up, and if loan rates are fixed the margin shrinks.

Marketing.q: How would you sell a tractor loan to a first-time borrower in a village?
Marketing.a: Explain the EMI in simple terms linked to harvest cash flows, use the local dealer and branch officer, and stress quick approval and the Mahindra name.

Marketing.q: How can Mahindra Finance grow beyond vehicle loans?
Marketing.a: Cross-sell SME, personal, home and insurance products to its 1.2 crore+ existing customers, using data and digital journeys.

HR.q: How would you keep field and collection staff motivated in rural areas?
HR.a: Clear incentives, local hiring, training in soft collection skills, digital tools to cut paperwork, and recognition for good performers.

Sales.a: Ask about the buyer's need and budget, show an affordable EMI, explain quick paperwork through the dealer, and offer insurance cover.

Operations.q: How can technology improve collections for a rural lender?
Operations.a: Digital payment links, reminders in local languages and data to spot early stress; Mahindra Finance says it uses AI tools and regional language bots for collections.

Other.q: What does the housing-finance merger mean for the company?
Other.a: Vehicle, rural and home loans would sit in one listed company, cutting duplicate costs and letting it offer home loans to existing customers.

interview.why_us: Mahindra Finance started by helping rural buyers get loans for Mahindra vehicles, and today serves over 1.2 crore customers, many of them in villages and small towns. It is growing fast, with profit up 55% in Q2 FY27, and is adding home, SME and personal loans. Working here means learning lending at the grassroots and seeing how credit changes lives. I want to contribute to [your role] as it grows.
ask: How is the company balancing vehicle loans with newer products like SME and home loans?
What will change for customers and teams after the housing-finance merger?
What does success look like for a new joiner in the first six months?

gd.t: Should NBFCs lend to rural borrowers with no credit history?
gd.for: It brings credit to people banks ignore and helps them buy tractors and vehicles that earn income.
gd.against: Risk of bad loans is higher and depends on harvests and incomes.

gd.t: Should a group-owned lender mainly finance its parent's products?
gd.for: It boosts the parent's sales and the lender knows the products and dealers well.
gd.against: Too much dependence on one brand limits growth; lenders need wider portfolios.

Don't call it a bank; it is an NBFC and cannot take savings account deposits.
Don't mix standalone (₹882 cr) and consolidated (₹911 cr) Q2 FY27 profit; say which one you quote.
